clinicalPearls: In crossed renal ectopia one kidney lies on the side opposite its ureteric insertion; the crossed kidney sits contralaterally while its ureter still enters the bladder on the original side, crossing the midline

Fusion of the crossed kidney to the orthotopic kidney occurs in the great majority of cases, and several morphological types are described including unilateral fused ectopia, sigmoid or S-shaped, L-shaped or tandem, and lump or disc kidneys
Left-to-right crossing is the more frequent pattern, and the crossed kidney is usually inferior, malrotated and supplied by anomalous vessels arising from the nearby aorta or iliac arteries
Most cases are asymptomatic incidental findings; when symptomatic, the features stem from urinary stasis, namely infection, calculi and obstruction, particularly at the pelviureteric junction

Malrotation and a variable, aberrant blood supply make surgery technically demanding and increase the risk of pelviureteric junction obstruction, and the ectopic mass can be mistaken for an abdominal or pelvic tumour

It is associated with vesicoureteric reflux and with skeletal, cardiac, anorectal and genital anomalies, and sits within the wider spectrum of renal fusion and ectopia that includes the horseshoe kidney
A solitary crossed fused ectopic kidney represents the patient's entire functioning renal mass and therefore warrants protection and appropriate counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Crossed fused renal ectopia arises from an error during the ascent and rotation of the metanephric kidneys. Abnormal migration of one nephrogenic blastema, or malpositioning of its ureteric bud, causes one developing kidney to cross the midline; contact between the two renal masses before rotation and encapsulation are complete then leads to their fusion. Because the ureter of the crossed kidney was already committed to its side of origin, it continues to enter the bladder orthotopically even though the parenchyma now lies contralaterally. The malrotation, abnormal hilar orientation and aberrant blood supply from local vessels reflect the abnormal position of the kidney when it acquired its vasculature, and the resulting distorted drainage predisposes to stasis, reflux, infection and stone formation.
additionalDifferentials: Simple renal ectopia (pelvic kidney) without crossing
Unilateral renal agenesis with compensatory hypertrophy
Retroperitoneal or pelvic mass or tumour
Other renal fusion variants such as a lump or pancake kidney
additionalInvestigations: Renal tract ultrasound showing an empty renal fossa with both moieties on one side
Contrast-enhanced CT or CT/MR urography to define the fusion type, rotation and vascular supply before any surgery
MAG3 or DMSA scintigraphy for differential function and drainage
Micturating cystourethrogram where vesicoureteric reflux is suspected
Assessment for associated skeletal, cardiac and genital anomalies
Metabolic stone work-up when calculi are present
redFlags: Febrile urinary tract infection, pyelonephritis or urosepsis
Pelviureteric junction obstruction with pain or deteriorating function
Impaired function in a solitary crossed fused ectopic kidney
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent in the asymptomatic majority, with normal renal function and life expectancy. It worsens only if complications such as obstruction, recurrent infection or stones damage the parenchyma, which is more consequential when the fused unit constitutes solitary functioning renal tissue.
pitfalls: Mistaking the ectopic fused renal mass for a tumour or lymphadenopathy on imaging
Misinterpreting the empty renal fossa as unilateral renal agenesis
Overlooking the anomalous and variable blood supply during surgery and risking haemorrhage
Attributing loin pain solely to stones without assessing for pelviureteric junction obstruction
Failing to recognise and protect solitary functioning renal tissue
management: Manage the asymptomatic incidental majority conservatively with observation and reassurance
Treat urinary tract infections promptly with appropriate antibiotics and manage calculi with lithotripsy or endourological techniques
Relieve pelviureteric junction obstruction surgically with pyeloplasty, planning any operation around detailed cross-sectional and vascular imaging given the aberrant blood supply
Manage associated vesicoureteric reflux with antibiotic prophylaxis or antireflux surgery as indicated
Undertake surveillance of renal function and imaging for stones, obstruction and hydronephrosis, with heightened vigilance when the fused unit is the solitary functioning renal tissue
Institute a metabolic stone-prevention work-up and dietary measures where calculi recur
Assess for and manage associated skeletal, cardiac, anorectal and genital anomalies through appropriate specialists
